## The two partitions coincide

- ratio: deficit 0.487--0.768, parity 1.003--1.039
- graph-arm CV: deficit 3.73--13.92%, parity 0.82--1.95% (disjoint: True)
- gap between the two ratio groups: **0.235**
- same partition: **True**, p = **0.008** under random assignment (exactly 1/120 = 0.0083, the chance that the 3 highest-dispersion sessions of 10 are exactly the 3 lowest-ratio ones)

Both axes are within-session, so neither can be produced by a card-level offset that moves both arms together (F034).

The driver is therefore not sufficient on its own, and on Modal a driver change cannot happen without a change to the sandbox that proxies the driver -- so what F042 calls the driver may be the sandbox.

## Which predicts the regime better: the release, or the date?

F040 withdrew the engine-release reading and named calendar date as a confound it could not separate. Tested directly on the same sessions, date is the better predictor. The cut is chosen post hoc, so these are two hypotheses compared on identical data, not a test of either.

| predictor | split | one-sided Fisher p |
|---|---|---|
| engine release (0.29.0 vs later) | 3/7 vs 0/3 | **0.292** |
| date within 0.29.0 (before 10-31 vs on/after) | 3/3 vs 0/4 | **0.029** |
| date, all engines (before 10-31 vs on/after) | 3/5 vs 0/5 | **0.083** |

With 3 against 4, 0.029 is the smallest p reachable, so a perfect split scores the floor and nothing stronger is obtainable at this sample size.

**Prediction, recorded before the next run.** One further 0.29.0 session after 10-31 landing in parity takes the date reading to p = **0.018**. One landing in deficit refutes it outright. The practical consequence: if the deficit regime has stopped occurring on this provider's fleet, waiting for one to appear is not a plan, and the open mechanism question cannot be closed by spending more.

## Is the deficit associated with the engine release?

3 of 7 sessions on vllm-0.29.0 against 0 of 3 on later releases. One-sided Fisher exact **p = 0.292**.

Across all L4 sessions the releases are indistinguishable. That comparison mixes two host drivers, and F042 shows the split is clean within one: on driver 580.95.05, 0.29.0 is deficient 3/3 and 0.30.0 0/2. The engine-release reading is conditional on the driver, not withdrawn.

Pooling every fixed-prompt default-arm boot gives n = **128**: 44 deficit boots spanning 29.5--65.6 tok/s and 84 parity boots spanning 75.5--83.9 tok/s.

- groups overlap: **False**
- gap between groups: **9.9** tok/s
- largest gap within either group: 5.7 tok/s

Deficit graph arms clock **177--291 MHz higher** than any parity graph arm while producing 18.8--26.9 tok/s fewer, drawing less power and being capped less often. A card that boosts higher and delivers less work is not at a power ceiling. Utilisation sampling was added after the last deficit session, so the stall reading this implies is still untested.

## Is the regime speculative, or a CUDA-graph property?

Sessions that measured both mechanisms inside ONE container. A session measuring only one mechanism is absent rather than listed blank: a missing arm is silence, not a null result.

| session | engine | dflash ratio | none ratio | dflash CV | none CV | reading |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 11-01T12-30 | vllm-0.29.0 | **1.012** | **1.034** | 0.82% | 0.14% | parity session, separates nothing |

0 of 1 sessions are decisive; the rest are parity sessions, which separate the two readings not at all.

## What the n-gram comparison can still support

The draft-model localisation (F018) rests on two n-gram sessions being quiet. Both sat in the parity regime. At the observed deficit frequency of 3 in 10, two sessions both land in parity with probability (7/10)^2 = **0.49** even if n-gram is affected exactly as dflash is. Two quiet n-gram sessions are therefore an unremarkable outcome under the null, and the localisation needs n-gram measured inside a deficit session.
